parts.title: My first part in a play
parts.instructions: Read the text and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When my friend asked me to join the Garrow Quay Players last spring, I laughed. I had never been on a stage, apart from a school concert when I was ten. I was the girl who forgot the words of a song and ran off in tears. But she said they needed someone to play a small part, a postman with just three lines, and she promised that I would not have to dance.

Rehearsals were on Tuesday and Thursday evenings in an old hall above a bakery. I was terrified at first, but the other actors were so welcoming that I soon relaxed. The director kept telling me to speak more slowly, because when I am nervous I talk very fast. I practised my three lines in the shower, on the bus and even while walking my dog.

On the first night I felt sick. Through the curtain I could see that every seat was full, including two in the front row for my parents. But the moment I stepped onto the stage, something changed. The lights were so bright that I could not see anybody, so it felt as if I was alone, talking to my own front door. I said my lines perfectly, and when people laughed in the right place, it was the best feeling in the world.

Now I help with the costumes as well, and I have been offered a bigger part in the next play. I am not sure that I am ready, but I am going to say yes.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer laugh at the invitation?
options: She thought the play sounded boring.
She did not have enough free time.
She remembered a bad experience on stage.
She was too old to learn acting.
questions.explanation: She had been on stage only once, at ten, when she forgot the words and ran off in tears.

questions.prompt: What did the director often tell the writer to do?
questions.explanation: The director kept telling her to speak more slowly because she talks fast when nervous.

questions.prompt: How did she feel just before the first performance?
options: Confident because her parents were there
questions.explanation: She says she felt sick on the first night and saw the full theatre through the curtain.

questions.prompt: Why did she feel less afraid on the stage?
options: The director told her to be brave.
She could not see the audience.
She knew all the other actors very well.
Her parents smiled at her from the front row.
questions.explanation: The lights were so bright that she could not see anybody and felt alone.

questions.prompt: What is she going to do next?
questions.explanation: She has been offered a bigger part and says she is going to say yes.

parts.title: A student film festival
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Every year in June, the students of Garrow Quay College organise a film festival. This year it took place over a long weekend, and I was one of the volunteers. [1] I spent most of the first day carrying chairs and fixing posters to doors, so I was not expecting to enjoy it much.

On Friday evening, the first films were shown in the college theatre. All of them were made by students, and none was longer than ten minutes. [2] One was about a boy and his grandmother's garden, and it made half the audience cry. Another was a silly comedy filmed entirely in a supermarket at night.

On Saturday, a well-known film director came to give a talk. [3] He said he had made his first film on his father's old camera when he was fourteen, and that nobody could teach you to tell a story better than making mistakes. [4] I wrote that down, and many other people did too.

The winners were announced on Sunday afternoon. The prize for best film went to a group of first-year students, who had made a film about a lost dog. [5] I hope next year I will be brave enough to enter a film of my own.
sentences: That was why she had decided to make films about animals.
They were much better than I had imagined.
The college theatre was built more than fifty years ago.
It was the first time I had worked at such a big event.
I thought that was the best advice of the whole weekend.
Everyone clapped loudly, even the people whose films had not won.
He was friendly and spoke in a very simple way, which the students liked.
She is also the head of the drama department.

gaps.explanation: Sentence F explains why the writer was a volunteer without experience; "I spent most of the first day carrying chairs" continues the idea.
"They were much better than I had imagined" refers to the student films and leads to the examples that follow.
Sentence A describes the director who gave the talk; "He said he had made his first film" continues with "he".
"I thought that was the best advice" refers to the point about making mistakes, and the next sentence says "I wrote that down".
Sentence B shows the audience's reaction to the winners and leads to the writer's hope for next year. Sentence D is about the building and fits nowhere.

parts.title: A review of a TV series
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: I have just finished watching the first series of Harbour Lights, and I would [1] it to anyone who likes mysteries. The story is [2] in a small fishing town, where a young police officer is trying to find out who has been stealing boats. Each episode lasts forty minutes, so it is easy to [3] one more before bed. The actors are very good, especially the woman who plays the officer's grandmother, who is [4] and moving at the same time. Some viewers [5] that the ending is too fast, but I enjoyed it. I am already looking forward to the second series, which will be [6] next spring.

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: "Recommend it to anyone" is the natural pattern; "advise", "propose" and "offer" do not fit.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: A story is "set in" a place.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: You watch an episode; take, make and join do not fit.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: "Funny and moving at the same time" is a positive description that matches the praise for the actors.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: "Complain that the ending is too fast" fits the criticism; "refuse", "wonder" and "promise" do not take this pattern.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: A series is shown on television; it is not won or kept.

parts.title: A message about going to the cinema
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Hi Gordon,
Are you free on Friday evening? I would love to [1] to the cinema to see the new film about the pilot. It starts [2] 7.45 p.m. at the Quay Cinema, [3] I think we should meet at 7.15, because there [4] usually a long queue for tickets. If you [5] rather go on Saturday, that is fine as well. Do you remember [6] we saw a film together? It was last summer, and we both laughed so much!
Layla

gaps.explanation: "Would love to go to the cinema" uses the infinitive after "would love to"; "come" also fits.
We say a film starts "at" a time; "around" or "about" is also possible.
"So" shows the reason for meeting early.
"There is usually a long queue" is the present simple of "there is".
"If you would rather go" is the fixed pattern for expressing a preference.
"Remember when we saw a film together" introduces the time of the memory.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: bushra
turns.text: Garrow Quay Playhouse, Bushra speaking. How can I help?

turns.speaker: percy
turns.text: Hello. I’d like tickets for Saturday afternoon’s show, please. One for me and one for my daughter. She’s four.

turns.speaker: bushra
turns.text: An adult ticket is twelve pounds. For children between five and sixteen it’s six pounds.

turns.speaker: percy
turns.text: Oh, I thought I’d pay six for her. That’s what we paid for her brother last winter.

turns.speaker: bushra
turns.text: Well, she’s under five, so she can sit on your knee, and we charge nothing for that. You only pay for yourself.

turns.speaker: percy
turns.text: That’s great news. So it’s just the twelve pounds.

turns.speaker: bushra
turns.text: Yes. Shall I take your card number now?

question.prompt: How much will Percy pay for his daughter's ticket?
question.explanation: Six pounds is the price for children from five, and twelve pounds is for the adult, but Percy’s daughter is only four, so she sits on his knee and they charge nothing.

turns.speaker: jessica
turns.text: Zachary, I’m at the snack bar. Do you want the usual, a large popcorn and a big cola?

turns.speaker: zachary
turns.text: Not tonight. I nearly ordered that on Friday, but I felt terrible afterwards.

turns.speaker: jessica
turns.text: So a medium popcorn and a small cola?

turns.speaker: zachary

turns.speaker: jessica

turns.speaker: zachary

turns.speaker: jessica

options: Large popcorn and a big cola
Medium popcorn and a small cola

turns.speaker: naomi
turns.text: Sorry, sir, I can’t let you in without a ticket.

turns.speaker: emre
turns.text: I have one, but I left the paper at home. I booked online three weeks ago.

turns.speaker: naomi
turns.text: I could print a new one at the desk, but that costs two pounds.

turns.speaker: emre
turns.text: No, I’d rather not pay twice. I thought of asking my friend Hana to come out, but she’s already inside with her phone off.

turns.speaker: naomi
turns.text: Did they send you a confirmation?

turns.speaker: emre
turns.text: Yes, hold on. It’s still in my inbox. Look, here’s the booking number and my seat.

turns.speaker: naomi

question.prompt: How can Emre prove that he has a ticket?
options: By showing a message on his phone
By paying for a new ticket
By asking a friend to help

turns.speaker: fearghal
turns.text: Hi everyone, it’s Fearghal with a message about tomorrow’s rehearsal. We normally start at six, and that’s what I told you on Monday. But the school hall is being used for a concert until six, so I asked the caretaker if we could begin at five thirty in the small room. He said it’s closed for painting, sorry! So please come at six thirty instead, and bring your scripts. We’ll finish at nine at the latest. If you can’t come, text me tonight, because tomorrow I’ll be busy until the very last minute. See you then!

question.explanation: The usual time is six and the small room at five thirty is not available, so the rehearsal is moved to six thirty.

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: Which film shall we see on Saturday? Everyone says the new comedy is hilarious.

turns.speaker: alistair
turns.text: I saw the trailer. The jokes weren’t very funny, and the reviews are terrible.

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: Then what about the cartoon? My little cousin is coming with us.

turns.speaker: alistair
turns.text: Your cousin can come another day. The cartoon is for little kids, and he’s twelve.

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: True. So what do you want to see?

turns.speaker: alistair
turns.text: The one with the spaceship and the robots. I love science fiction. It’s long, but the special effects are amazing.

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: Okay, you win. I’ll book seats for eight o’clock.

question.explanation: The comedy has bad reviews and the cartoon is for little kids, so Alistair suggests the one with the spaceship and robots, which is the science-fiction film.

turns.speaker: dafydd
turns.text: Good evening, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to the Garrow Quay Playhouse. Before you take your seats, a few quick reminders. Some of you have large bags with you. In the past we asked everyone to leave them in the cloakroom, but there’s no need now, as long as they fit under your seat. You can buy a programme at the stalls in the foyer, but you don’t have to, because the cast list is on the screens. The most important thing is your mobile. Please put it on silent, not just vibrate, and keep it in your pocket during the show. The performance begins in ten minutes. Enjoy it!

question.prompt: What must the visitors do before they go in?
options: Buy a programme for the show
question.explanation: Bags only had to be left outside in the past and the programme is not necessary, but the speaker says the most important thing is to put your mobile on silent.

turns.speaker: martha
turns.text: Hi Manish, it’s Martha. I found the remote control at last! I know you looked on the shelf this morning, and I checked it again just to be sure, but it wasn’t there. Then I thought of the kitchen, because you were making tea earlier. I nearly gave up and bought a new one online. But when I moved the cushions to clean the living room, I saw it on the floor, right at the back, beneath the sofa. It was probably there since Sunday’s match. Anyway, I’ll leave it on the table. Call me when you get home. Bye!

question.explanation: The shelf and the kitchen did not have it; Martha saw it on the floor beneath the sofa when she moved the cushions.

parts.title: Understanding the main idea
parts.instructions: Listen to six short conversations and choose the best answer.

turns.speaker: amelia
turns.text: Wei, you went to the Rivers concert on Friday. How was it?

turns.speaker: wei
turns.text: The band was brilliant, and the show lasted two hours, so I can’t complain about that.

turns.speaker: amelia
turns.text: And was it expensive? I heard tickets were sixty pounds.

turns.speaker: wei
turns.text: I paid thirty because I booked early. No, my problem was different. I stood near the speakers, and my ears were ringing for two days.

turns.speaker: amelia
turns.text: Oh no! Could you hear the words at least?

turns.speaker: wei
turns.text: Hardly. Everything was a big noise. I won’t go again without ear plugs.

turns.speaker: amelia
turns.text: Next time we’ll stand at the back. Deal?

turns.speaker: wei
turns.text: Deal.

question.prompt: What did Wei think of the concert?
question.explanation: The show was long enough and the ticket cost thirty pounds, but Wei stood near the speakers, his ears rang for two days and he could hardly hear the words, so it was too loud.

turns.speaker: kirsty
turns.text: Are you watching the new reality show tonight, Meirion?

turns.speaker: meirion
turns.text: Not really. I watched one episode and that was enough.

turns.speaker: kirsty
turns.text: It’s two hours long, I know, but it teaches useful skills, like how to manage your money.

turns.speaker: meirion
turns.text: Length isn’t the problem. I can watch for hours. It’s that everything is planned. The producers tell people what to say, and the arguments are acted.

turns.speaker: kirsty
turns.text: Really? I thought the people were just being themselves.

turns.speaker: meirion
turns.text: I’ve read interviews with former contestants. There’s nothing genuine about it. It’s all a script.

turns.speaker: kirsty
turns.text: That’s a pity. I enjoy them anyway.

turns.speaker: meirion
turns.text: Fine, but I’d rather watch a documentary.

question.prompt: What does Meirion think about reality shows?
question.explanation: Kirsty mentions the length and useful skills, but Meirion says that the producers plan what people say and that the arguments are acted, so he thinks the shows are not genuine.

turns.speaker: liam
turns.text: Have you seen the film of The Silver Road yet?

turns.speaker: thandi
turns.text: Not yet. I read the book last year and I’m not sure I want to.

turns.speaker: liam
turns.text: Why not? The film is only ninety minutes, and the book took you weeks.

turns.speaker: thandi
turns.text: Speed doesn’t matter to me. And I don’t think the film is boring. The reviews are good.

turns.speaker: liam
turns.text: So what’s the problem?

turns.speaker: thandi
turns.text: In the book I made my own pictures of the characters and the old house. I imagine everything differently from a director. When I see actors, those pictures disappear.

turns.speaker: liam
turns.text: I never thought of that. I like seeing it all at once.

turns.speaker: thandi
turns.text: Good for you. For me, the best images are in my head, so I’ll stay with the book.

question.prompt: Why does Thandi prefer the book to the film?
options: It is quicker to finish than a film.
The film is too long and boring.
She can imagine the story herself.
question.explanation: The film is shorter and the reviews are good, but Thandi likes the pictures she creates in her head when she reads, and the film would replace them.

turns.speaker: dafydd
turns.text: Jessica, are you okay? You keep moving in your seat.

turns.speaker: jessica
turns.text: Honestly, no. Can we change seats?

turns.speaker: dafydd
turns.text: Is it the screen? It’s very bright tonight.

turns.speaker: jessica
turns.text: It’s not that, I like it big. It’s the front row. I have to look up all the time and my neck hurts.

turns.speaker: dafydd
turns.text: I see. There are two seats in row F, but they’re far from Amira and the others.

turns.speaker: jessica
turns.text: I don’t mind if I sit with them or not. I’d rather be comfortable.

turns.speaker: dafydd

turns.speaker: jessica

She wants to sit with a friend.

parts.title: A talk about a summer theatre programme
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: ashleigh
turns.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Garrow Quay Playhouse. I am Ashleigh, the manager, and I’d like to tell you about our summer programme. It begins in June. We had planned to start in May, but the roof needed repairs, so the first night is on the second of June. Now, about the evenings. The shows start at half past seven, and the doors open one hour before that, at half past six, so you can have a drink in the cafe. Some people think we open at five, but that’s only for the staff. Let me tell you about the shows. Our opening show is a musical about a sailor coming home after many years. We first thought of a comedy for the opening night, but the musical was a better choice, because the songs are wonderful. Later in July there will be a comedy, and in August we have a detective play. Now, about tickets. A normal ticket is fifteen pounds. Students pay half the normal price on Tuesdays and Wednesdays, just show your card at the door. On Thursdays, people over sixty-five get a smaller discount, but it isn’t half. We also have free workshops on Saturday mornings. They are for children between six and ten, and they learn to make masks and to move on stage. Teenagers can join a drama club, but that’s on Sunday afternoons and it isn’t free. Finally, how to book. You can book online, which is the cheapest way, or you can come to the box office, next to the main door. It’s open from ten until six, every day. We used to sell tickets in the cafe, but we stopped that last year. If you have any questions, please ask me, or any of my colleagues. Thank you for listening, and I hope to see you all this summer.

gaps.prompt: The first night of the summer season is in ___
gaps.explanation: She says the season begins in June; May was the earlier plan, before the roof repairs.

gaps.prompt: Visitors can come into the theatre one ___ before a show starts
gaps.explanation: Doors open one hour before the show, at half past six; five o’clock is only for the staff.

gaps.prompt: The first show of the summer is a ___ about a sailor coming home
gaps.explanation: The opening show is a musical; a comedy was the first idea but the musical was better, and the comedy comes in July.

gaps.prompt: Students pay half the normal ___ on Tuesdays and Wednesdays

parts.title: An interview with a stage actor
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Llewellyn, how did you first get interested in acting?

turns.speaker: llewellyn
turns.text: It wasn’t a school trip, though we went to a pantomime once and I was bored. A teacher did tell me to try the drama club, but I said no, I preferred football. Then I broke my leg at fifteen and stayed at home for two months. My aunt gave me a pile of old plays, and I read them all, doing the voices. That’s when I fell in love with it.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What’s the hardest thing about stage work?

turns.speaker: llewellyn
turns.text: Everyone expects it to be the lines, but I’m quite good at that. I just repeat them on the bus. The other actors are lovely too, we’re like a family. The difficult bit is the hundredth night. You say the same words again, and you must make them sound new, as if it were the first time. When I get it right, it’s magic.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about the night when your beard fell off. How did you feel?

turns.speaker: llewellyn
turns.text: It was a serious scene, and in the middle of my speech half of it dropped on the floor. For a second I wanted to run off the stage, and I thought about stopping the show. But then I decided it didn’t matter. I picked it up, put it in my pocket and carried on as if it was part of the plan. The audience clapped at the end.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why do you prefer the theatre to film?

turns.speaker: llewellyn
turns.text: The money is better in films, I won’t pretend it isn’t, and the hours on a film set are longer. But on a film set you do the scene ten times and then it’s finished. In the theatre it’s live, and anything can happen. A phone rings, someone forgets a line. That danger keeps me alert, and I love it.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: And how do you relax before a show?

turns.speaker: llewellyn
turns.text: People think I eat a lot, but I never eat before a show, I’d feel sick. I do practise my lines for an hour, but with the whole cast, in the corridor, not alone. Then, ten minutes before, I sing a silly song to myself in the dressing room, always the same one about a duck. It makes me laugh and my nerves disappear.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What advice would you give to young people?

turns.speaker: llewellyn
turns.text: Don’t wait for a phone call with a great part, it may never come. Drama schools are good, but they’re expensive, and you don’t need years there to start. I’d say, find a local group. You learn how to work with others, how to build scenery, you make friends, and you get on stage every month. That’s how I really began.
